title: IV Insulin Infusion: Glucose and Potassium Together
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Continuous IV insulin can change glucose and potassium quickly. Safe care requires protocol-based pump use, frequent glucose checks, potassium surveillance, and immediate response to hypoglycemia or rapidly falling potassium rather than focusing on glucose alone.
recognize: Insulin shifts potassium into cells and can unmask or worsen total-body potassium depletion.
An unexpectedly rapid glucose fall can reflect excessive infusion, interruption of nutrition/dextrose, or a pump/line error.
priorities: Verify the exact insulin product, concentration, pump channel, and protocol.
Check glucose at the protocol-defined frequency and review potassium/renal status.
Escalate hypoglycemia, severe hypokalemia, pump interruption, or altered mental status immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend bedside glucose, potassium, ECG when clinically indicated, intake/nutrition, renal function, neurologic status, and infusion continuity.
interventions: Use dedicated or clearly traced tubing according to facility policy.
Coordinate dextrose/nutrition changes with insulin adjustments under the protocol.
medicationSafety: IV insulin is a high-alert medication and requires independent verification where policy requires.
Do not stop insulin in DKA simply because glucose has normalized if ketoacidosis has not resolved; follow the DKA protocol.
teaching: Explain why frequent finger-stick or blood glucose checks are required during the infusion.
delegationScope: Insulin-infusion titration authority varies by state/facility and requires validated competency; abnormal trends require licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Adjusting IV insulin from glucose alone while ignoring falling potassium.
oneLinePearl: IV insulin moves two numbers at once: glucose and potassium.

title: Heparin Infusion: Protocol, Bleeding, and HIT
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Continuous unfractionated heparin requires a validated weight/order protocol, pump controls, and laboratory monitoring. New bleeding, major hemoglobin drop, thrombocytopenia, or new thrombosis can indicate serious complications including HIT.
recognize: Heparin effect may be monitored with aPTT or anti-Xa depending on the protocol.
HIT is a prothrombotic immune complication; a falling platelet count plus new thrombosis is especially concerning.
priorities: Verify patient weight used by the order, concentration, pump rate, and latest monitoring result.
Assess for overt and occult bleeding.
Escalate suspected HIT or major bleeding immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend aPTT/anti-Xa as ordered, CBC/platelets, hemoglobin, bleeding, new thrombosis symptoms, renal/hepatic context, and infusion continuity.
interventions: Use independent double checks where required.
Follow the protocol exactly for holds, rate changes, and repeat labs rather than improvising.
medicationSafety: Heparin is high-alert and multiple vial/bag concentrations can create serious error risk.
Do not administer IM because of hematoma risk.
teaching: Report black stool, severe headache, blood in urine, unusual bruising, or new limb/chest symptoms promptly.
delegationScope: Heparin-infusion management authority varies by state/facility; protocol interpretation and adverse-event assessment require licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Increasing heparin because the lab looks low without checking whether the infusion was paused, infiltrated, or drawn from a contaminated line.
oneLinePearl: Heparin safety is protocol fidelity plus bleeding and platelet surveillance.

title: 3% Hypertonic Saline: Sodium Correction Under Control
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hypertonic saline is a high-osmolar sodium solution used in selected severe hyponatremia and neurologic situations. The danger is overcorrection, fluid overload, and local vascular injury; serum sodium and neurologic status must be trended closely according to the prescribed correction plan.
recognize: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia may cause seizure, confusion, vomiting, or reduced consciousness.
Too-rapid sodium correction can cause osmotic demyelination.
priorities: Verify solution concentration and indication before starting.
Use the prescribed access route/pump and obtain sodium checks at the ordered frequency.
Escalate unexpectedly rapid sodium rise, new neurologic deficits, or pulmonary edema.
assessMonitor: Trend sodium, neurologic status, fluid balance, lung sounds, BP, urine output, and IV-site condition.
interventions: Follow a controlled correction strategy rather than attempting immediate normalization.
Maintain seizure precautions when clinically indicated.
medicationSafety: 3% and 5% sodium chloride are hypertonic products and must not be confused with routine 0.9% saline.
Access requirements vary by concentration, rate, and facility policy.
teaching: Explain that frequent blood tests are needed because safe correction is deliberately controlled.
delegationScope: Hypertonic-saline infusion management requires facility-defined competency; neurologic and sodium-trend assessment remains licensed-nurse responsibility.
examTrap: Trying to normalize severe hyponatremia as fast as possible once symptoms improve.
oneLinePearl: With hypertonic saline, controlled correction is the treatment.

title: IV Magnesium Replacement: Rhythm and Reflex Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV magnesium replacement can stabilize dangerous deficiency but excessive or rapid administration can cause flushing, hypotension, loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, and cardiac conduction problems. Renal function and the clinical indication determine how cautiously it must be given.
recognize: Hypomagnesemia can contribute to tremor, weakness, seizures, and ventricular dysrhythmias including torsades.
Kidney dysfunction increases magnesium accumulation risk.
priorities: Verify magnesium level, renal function, indication, concentration, and ordered rate.
Monitor rhythm and hemodynamics when severe deficiency or rapid replacement is involved.
Escalate respiratory depression, absent reflexes, marked hypotension, or bradycardia.
assessMonitor: Trend magnesium, potassium/calcium when relevant, renal function, respiratory status, reflexes in high-exposure settings, and ECG/rhythm.
interventions: Use pump-controlled infusion and appropriate dilution/rate per product and facility guidance.
medicationSafety: Magnesium sulfate formulations/concentrations differ.
Replacement should not be treated as interchangeable with obstetric seizure-prophylaxis protocols.
teaching: Explain that repeat labs may be needed because magnesium and potassium abnormalities often coexist.
delegationScope: IV magnesium administration authority varies by state/facility; toxicity assessment requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Giving rapid magnesium replacement to a patient with severe renal failure without adjusting the plan.
oneLinePearl: Replace magnesium, but respect the kidneys and the respiratory system.

title: IV Sodium Phosphate: Replace Phosphorus, Count Sodium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sodium phosphate is a concentrated IV phosphorus source that must be diluted before administration. Safe replacement requires attention to phosphorus, calcium, sodium, renal function, and infusion rate because rapid or excessive replacement can cause hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and calcium-phosphate complications.
recognize: Severe hypophosphatemia can cause weakness, respiratory muscle failure, hemolysis, or impaired cardiac function.
The sodium content matters in patients with heart, kidney, or volume problems.
priorities: Verify current phosphorus, calcium, sodium, renal function, and the ordered amount/rate.
Ensure the concentrated product is diluted exactly as required.
Escalate symptomatic hypocalcemia, arrhythmia, severe weakness, or renal deterioration.
assessMonitor: Trend phosphorus, calcium, sodium, potassium, renal function, respiratory strength, and ECG when clinically indicated.
interventions: Use pump-controlled infusion and compatibility checks.
medicationSafety: Current 2026 labels identify sodium phosphate injection as concentrated additive therapy for diluted IV fluids.
Choose sodium versus potassium phosphate based on the entire electrolyte picture, not phosphorus alone.
teaching: Explain why repeat electrolyte testing is required after IV replacement.
delegationScope: Concentrated-electrolyte preparation/administration requires facility-defined competency and verification.
examTrap: Choosing sodium phosphate without checking whether the patient already has sodium/volume overload.
oneLinePearl: Phosphate replacement also gives you a cation—count the sodium.
sourceBasis: DailyMed sodium phosphates injection labeling updated 2026-05

title: Esmolol Infusion: Fast Beta Blockade, Fast Reassessment
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Esmolol is an ultra-short-acting IV beta blocker used when rapid, titratable heart-rate or blood-pressure control is needed. Its short action makes effects reversible quickly, but bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, bronchospasm, and worsening heart failure still require immediate recognition.
recognize: Rate slowing can improve tachycardia but may reduce cardiac output if overdone.
Patients with conduction disease or severe reactive-airway disease need extra caution.
priorities: Monitor ECG, BP, symptoms, and perfusion continuously during titration.
Verify the ordered target rather than treating a number in isolation.
Escalate symptomatic bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, or bronchospasm.
assessMonitor: Trend heart rate/rhythm, BP, chest pain, dyspnea, mental status, urine output, and signs of heart failure.
interventions: Use controlled infusion equipment and approved titration protocol.
medicationSafety: Do not stack esmolol with other AV-node blockers without recognizing additive bradycardia/hypotension risk.
Current product labeling revised in 2026 should guide administration.
teaching: Explain that the medication acts and wears off quickly, so continuous monitoring is necessary.
delegationScope: Titrated beta-blocker infusion management requires defined facility/state competency.
examTrap: Increasing esmolol because the heart rate remains high while the blood pressure and perfusion are already falling.
oneLinePearl: Esmolol is fast on and fast off—reassess just as fast.
sourceBasis: DailyMed esmolol hydrochloride injection labeling revised 2026-03

title: IV Diltiazem: Rate Control Without Losing Perfusion
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV diltiazem slows AV nodal conduction and is used for selected supraventricular tachyarrhythmias. It can cause hypotension, bradycardia, or AV block and may worsen some forms of decompensated systolic heart failure, so stability must be checked before and during therapy.
recognize: Rate control is not appropriate as a substitute for immediate synchronized cardioversion when tachyarrhythmia is causing hemodynamic instability.
Concurrent beta blockers or other AV-node blockers can intensify rate slowing.
priorities: Assess stability, BP, rhythm, chest pain, dyspnea, and heart-failure signs before administration.
Monitor ECG and BP during IV therapy.
Escalate hypotension, high-grade block, severe bradycardia, or worsening pulmonary edema.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm/rate, BP, perfusion, lung sounds, oxygenation, and response to therapy.
interventions: Use pump-controlled infusion for continuous therapy and follow the ordered rate-control target.
medicationSafety: Avoid giving IV diltiazem reflexively to every rapid rhythm; identify the rhythm and stability first.
Current injection labeling was updated in 2026.
teaching: Explain that the drug slows conduction and may require continuous cardiac monitoring.
delegationScope: IV antiarrhythmic/rate-control infusion authority varies by state/facility and requires monitoring competency.
examTrap: Giving diltiazem to an unstable tachycardic patient instead of escalating for emergency rhythm management.
oneLinePearl: With IV diltiazem, control the rate without sacrificing pressure or perfusion.
sourceBasis: DailyMed diltiazem hydrochloride injection labeling updated 2026-05

title: IV Lidocaine: Ventricular Rhythm and Neurotoxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV lidocaine can suppress selected life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias but excessive levels can cause neurologic toxicity, seizures, bradycardia, conduction disturbance, and cardiovascular depression. Continuous ECG plus neurologic assessment is essential during infusion.
recognize: Early toxicity can include circumoral numbness, tinnitus, confusion, tremor, or drowsiness before seizure/cardiovascular collapse.
Hepatic dysfunction or low cardiac output can reduce clearance and raise toxicity risk.
priorities: Monitor ECG, BP, mental status, and neurologic symptoms.
Verify the antiarrhythmic formulation/concentration rather than confusing it with local-anesthetic products.
Escalate new neurologic toxicity, seizure, bradycardia, or widening conduction abnormalities.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm, BP, neurologic status, hepatic function/context, and infusion rate.
interventions: Use controlled infusion equipment and the prescribed arrhythmia protocol.
medicationSafety: Different lidocaine products/concentrations are used for local anesthesia versus antiarrhythmic therapy.
Neurologic symptoms may precede severe toxicity.
teaching: Tell conscious patients to report ringing in the ears, numbness around the mouth, unusual taste, dizziness, or confusion.
delegationScope: IV antiarrhythmic infusion administration/titration requires facility-defined competency and state authorization.
examTrap: Ignoring new tinnitus and confusion because the cardiac rhythm has improved.
oneLinePearl: Lidocaine can quiet the ventricle and irritate the brain—watch both.
sourceBasis: DailyMed lidocaine hydrochloride antiarrhythmic injection labeling

title: Phentolamine: Adrenergic Extravasation Rescue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Phentolamine is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist used in selected vasopressor extravasation protocols to reverse local vasoconstriction. The key nursing action is rapid recognition of extravasation, stopping the offending infusion, preserving access for aspiration when protocol directs, and activating the drug-specific rescue pathway.
recognize: Pain, blanching, coolness, swelling, delayed capillary refill, or skin discoloration near a vasopressor IV can signal extravasation.
Tissue ischemia can progress if vasoconstriction persists.
priorities: Stop the vasopressor infusion and assess the site/perfusion immediately.
Follow the facility extravasation protocol, including whether to aspirate through the existing catheter before removal.
Notify pharmacy/provider/RN team and obtain phentolamine promptly when indicated.
assessMonitor: Trend site color, temperature, pain, swelling, capillary refill, distal perfusion, and response after antidote treatment.
interventions: Administer local antidote only according to the approved infiltration protocol and competency.
medicationSafety: The rescue method is drug- and protocol-specific; do not apply one extravasation approach to every medication.
Delayed recognition increases tissue-injury risk.
teaching: Tell patients receiving peripheral vasopressors to report burning, pain, coolness, or swelling immediately.
delegationScope: Extravasation assessment and antidote infiltration require licensed-nurse/provider/pharmacy protocol and state/facility competency.
examTrap: Removing the IV immediately before checking whether the protocol needs the catheter for aspiration or antidote delivery.
oneLinePearl: Vasopressor extravasation is a tissue-perfusion emergency—stop, assess, rescue fast.

title: IV Potassium Phosphate: Phosphorus Plus Potassium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Potassium phosphate replaces phosphorus while also delivering potassium. Safe use requires checking both phosphorus and potassium, along with calcium and kidney function, because hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and arrhythmias can result from inappropriate replacement.
recognize: Renal impairment increases both potassium and phosphate accumulation risk.
A patient with hypophosphatemia may still have normal or high potassium, making potassium phosphate the wrong replacement choice.
priorities: Verify phosphorus, potassium, calcium, renal function, concentration, dilution, and ordered rate.
Use pump-controlled infusion and required compatibility checks.
Escalate ECG changes, symptomatic hypocalcemia, or worsening renal function.
assessMonitor: Trend phosphorus, potassium, calcium, creatinine, ECG when indicated, and clinical muscle/respiratory function.
interventions: Choose sodium versus potassium phosphate based on the full electrolyte pattern and order.
medicationSafety: Current 2026 labeling warns of hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia and requires monitoring during/following infusion.
Concentrated formulations require dilution before IV administration.
teaching: Explain why several electrolytes are rechecked after replacement, not phosphorus alone.
delegationScope: Concentrated-electrolyte IV administration requires facility/state competency and independent verification where required.
examTrap: Choosing potassium phosphate solely because phosphorus is low while potassium is already elevated.
oneLinePearl: Potassium phosphate replaces two things—so monitor two things.
sourceBasis: DailyMed potassium phosphates injection labeling updated 2026-07
